name: Creatine
summary: Creatine is a compound that muscles use to store quick energy for short, hard efforts. The body makes part of what it needs, mainly in the liver and kidneys, and the rest comes from meat and fish; about 95 % of it is stored in muscle. It is not an essential nutrient, but vegetarians, whose food contains almost none, have lower muscle stores.
roles: Stores quick energy in muscle as phosphocreatine, used in short bursts of hard effort
Carries energy from where cells make it to where they use it
Small amounts in the brain, which uses a lot of energy

status.note: There is no routine blood test for the body's creatine, and this app has no creatine marker. Research measures creatine in muscle from a small muscle sample (biopsy). Important for your results: about 1 to 2 % of the creatine in muscle turns into creatinine each day, and creatine supplements raise blood creatinine. The creatinine and eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate: kidney function worked out from creatinine) results in this app are based on that number. So a higher creatinine or a lower eGFR after starting creatine may not mean the kidneys are worse. It is worth telling the doctor about creatine before a kidney blood test.

signs: No clear signs in healthy people: the body makes its own creatine, and food adds the rest
Lower creatine stores in muscle with a diet that contains almost none (vegetarian or vegan)
Severe problems with the brain and nerves, and very low brain creatine, in rare inherited disorders of making or moving creatine
atRisk: Vegetarians and vegans: their food contains almost no creatine, and switching to a vegetarian diet lowered muscle creatine within 3 weeks to 3 months in trials
Children born with rare inherited disorders of creatine production or transport

signs: Weight gain of around a kilogram, mostly water, especially after high 'loading' amounts
Diarrhoea and stomach upset, more often with a large single amount
Higher blood creatinine and lower eGFR on kidney blood tests, without kidney damage in trials
high.note: Weight gain is the only side effect consistently reported in creatine research. In one trial in footballers, 10 g in one go caused diarrhoea more often (56 %) than the same amount as 5 g twice a day (29 %) or placebo (35 %). The International Society of Sports Nutrition reports that amounts up to 30 g a day for up to 5 years were safe and well tolerated in healthy people; several of its authors work with, or have received grants from, companies that sell creatine.

examples: Fish and seafood, such as salmon
foodSources.note: Plant foods contain almost no creatine. Eating meat and fish is different from taking isolated creatine monohydrate.

forms.name: Creatine monohydrate
forms.note: The form used in almost all research, including every trial in a 2024 meta-analysis on memory. It raises the creatine stored in muscle by about 15 to 40 %, and nearly all of it is either taken up by muscle or passes out in urine. Dry powder is stable; once mixed into a drink it slowly turns into creatinine, faster in acidic and warm drinks.

forms.name: Creatine hydrochloride (HCl), buffered creatine and other newer forms
forms.note: Sold as better absorbed or gentler on the stomach. Reviews in 2011 and 2022 found little or no evidence that any of them works better or is safer than monohydrate, which is the only form with substantial evidence for absorption, effect and safety.

forms.name: Creatine ethyl ester
forms.note: One of the newer forms. In a 2014 case report it raised blood creatinine to levels that looked like kidney failure in a person whose kidneys were normal; the results went back to normal after the supplement was stopped.

reference.noUpperLimit: Creatine is not an essential nutrient: the body makes its own and also gets it from meat and fish. So EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) has set no reference intake and no tolerable upper intake level for it. In 2004 EFSA assessed creatine monohydrate for use in foods for particular nutritional uses (such as sports foods); a 2022 review summarises that opinion as finding that up to 3 g a day of highly pure creatine, similar to the body's normal daily turnover, was unlikely to pose any risk. That is an amount judged safe, not a limit above which harm was seen. EFSA's later opinions are about health claims: in 2016 it accepted that creatine with regular resistance training improves muscle strength in adults over 55, and in 2024 it found that a link with better thinking has not been established.

interactions.note: Most trials were in healthy people. Creatine raises blood creatinine, which makes changes in kidney function harder to judge from the usual blood tests. With kidney disease, talk to your doctor before using creatine.

In trials creatine raised blood creatinine and lowered eGFR, while kidney filtration measured directly did not change. Telling the doctor about creatine helps them read the results; kidney function can also be measured with tests that do not rely on creatinine.

interactions.with: Medicines that are checked or dosed using kidney tests
interactions.note: Doctors use creatinine and eGFR to judge the kidneys when choosing doses of some medicines and when watching medicines that can affect the kidneys. A creatinine raised by creatine could be misread, so it is worth telling the doctor or pharmacist about creatine.
The trials summarised here did not study pregnant or breastfeeding women. Talk to your doctor or midwife before using creatine.

cautions: Creatine raises blood creatinine and lowers eGFR on kidney blood tests, without kidney damage in trials. Mention creatine to the doctor when kidney tests are done or read.
Weight often rises by around a kilogram, mostly as water, especially after high 'loading' amounts. It is not fat gain.
A large single amount causes diarrhoea more often: in one trial 10 g at once did, while the same amount split in two did not differ from placebo.

No form has been shown to work better than creatine monohydrate. Labels often promise more than the evidence: in a 2021 study of 167 creatine products sold online, only 25 % of the health claims met the criteria of EU rules and scientific reference documents.
The muscle benefits were seen together with resistance training: the trials compared training plus creatine with training alone.
Most trials lasted weeks to months; long-term trials are fewer.

commonUses: May increase strength and muscle size
May improve sprint and high-intensity exercise
May help keep muscle as you age

origin: The body makes creatine, mainly in the liver and kidneys, and gets the rest from meat and fish. About 95 % is stored in muscle, mostly as phosphocreatine, a quick energy reserve for short, hard efforts.
Supplement creatine is made industrially, not extracted from meat. Creatine monohydrate is the form with almost all the research.
dosage: EFSA has set no reference intake and no upper limit. A 2004 EFSA opinion found up to 3 g a day of highly pure creatine unlikely to pose a risk. This describes what was assessed, not a recommended amount.
Amounts commonly used in studies and supplements are about 5 to 7.5 g a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

Check the creatine content in grams on the label and that it is creatine monohydrate, and avoid adding together several products. Creatine raises blood creatinine, which affects kidney blood tests (see below).

targets.label: Amount EFSA's 2004 opinion found unlikely to pose a risk (highly pure creatine)
Amount commonly used in studies and supplements (5 g)
Amount commonly used in studies and supplements (7.5 g, the top of the usual range)

foods.name: Raw beef or salmon
foods.note: Reported as about 1–2 g of creatine per pound (454 g) of uncooked beef or salmon.

foodAmounts.verdict: Not practically. Food gives roughly 1–2 g per pound of raw meat or fish, so reaching 3 g needs about 0.7–1.4 kg of raw meat or fish every day, 5 g about 1.1–2.3 kg and 7.5 g about 1.7–3.4 kg. Cooking and the animal also change the amount. The body makes part of its creatine itself, and an ordinary meat-and-fish diet already supplies some of the rest; vegetarians eat almost none, so their muscle stores are lower.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Herring and some other fish are often quoted as richer in creatine, but this guide has no checked figure for them, so they are not in the table.
